A coordinated Majority World strategy is therefore essential to engage more assertively in international negotiations and to advocate for an AI governance framework that addresses existing asymmetries in AI capacity, influence and the equitable distribution of AI’s benefits.

articles.title: Why Nepal’s secular fabric is facing its toughest test yet
articles.summary:
The recent unrest in Tarai-Madhesh, triggered by a communal clash in Devanganj, Sunsari, on July 26, has reminded Nepal of its vulnerability to religious friction. The Nepali state has historically relied upon coercive force to maintain fragile peace. Such reactive measures are insufficient to address the undercurrents currently threatening the nation’s social fabric. It is now a matter of national urgency that the government initiates a rigorous and transparent investigation into the burgeoning influence and tactical operations of extremist religious outfits whose activities are increasingly linked to the propagation of religious hate in Nepal.

Nepal’s modern political identity was built upon a foundation of secular mobilisation, which has long existed in a state of tension with a historically Hinduised state structure. This friction has been exacerbated over the last decade, as political actors began instrumentalising religion for mobilisation. The rise of a religion-centric power structure in neighbouring states has further catalysed the shift in Nepal, empowering the religious organisations to mobilise resources across the border and expand their networks.

The methodology of this expansion warrants intense scrutiny. Alarmingly, current trends indicate the adoption of fluid organisational structures as a deliberate strategy to evade accountability. Rather than operating through identifiable entities, various groups are rapidly formed under innocuous banners only to be dissolved or rebranded once their immediate objectives of spreading religious rhetoric are achieved. This tactic, likely imported from contemporary practices in neighbouring states, makes it nearly impossible for journalists, researchers, or auditors to track funding sources and institutional affiliations. The state, therefore, seems to be the only mechanism capable of tracing the external influence on such organisations.

The reported involvement of retired high-ranking security officials, including former generals, with these religious-political organisations is another concern for national security. The recruitment of such individuals provides radical networks with tactical knowledge required to manipulate community-level violence. Meanwhile, the security apparatus remains characterised by an institutionalised insensitivity and a command mentality that prioritises punishment over dialogue. When the state relies on the indiscriminate use of force, coupled with former high-level security officials joining radical networks, it enables radical networks to use violence to rattle the social fabric.

The current administration’s failure to address the underlying causes of communal triggers is no longer tenable. The state’s historical amnesia regarding the roots of communal violence allows radical groups like the Hindu Samrat Sena to benefit from a fragmented landscape while maintaining links to extremist ideologies.

A meaningful response to this crisis requires more than traditional nationalist rhetoric, temporary curfews, or solidarity rallies. The authorities must empower the civil society of regional hubs, such as Biratnagar and Janakpur, to conduct autonomous investigations into communal incidents rather than waiting for orders from a centralised and often distracted leadership in Kathmandu. There must also be a concerted effort to foster an informed and critical citizenship capable of engaging in dialogue before tensions spiral into violence. Concurrently, the security forces need to be trained extensively in conflict de-escalation.

The preservation of Nepal’s secular identity demands that the state confront the opaque funding and fluid tactics of the organisations linked to extremist religious outfits. Failure to investigate these networks will only signal to the public—and to the international community—that the rule of law has been surrendered to the interests of imported religious radicalism.

articles.title: How Arya Nishaant uses AI as a catalyst for growth
articles.summary:
Creating efficiency

Artificial intelligence has become an invaluable tool in my journey of learning, creating, and growing. I don’t see AI as something that replaces my work but something that amplifies it. It allows me to work more efficiently. There are, of course, things it cannot do; it cannot replace the person you are, but it is helpful nonetheless.

Public appearances

Throughout my Miss Nepal journey, AI has been a trusted learning companion. It has helped me prepare for interviews, refine my speeches, and challenge my perspectives by encouraging me to think more deeply about my values, my advocacy, and the impact I hope to create. Rather than giving me answers, it has helped me ask better questions and articulate my own voice with greater clarity and confidence.

AI as an assistant

Professionally and academically, I use AI to organise ideas, simplify complex information, conduct research, and enhance presentations and written communication. By reducing the time spent on repetitive tasks, it allows me to dedicate more energy to meaningful work, strategic thinking, and human connection.

AI as a friend

Beyond work, AI fuels my curiosity. Whether I am exploring business and finance, discovering new books, seeking creative inspiration for art and fashion, or simply learning about the world, it encourages me to remain a lifelong learner. Every conversation becomes an opportunity to expand my perspective and deepen my understanding.

articles.title: Mental wellbeing: When a child becomes the caregiver
articles.summary:
Some children learn to read the room before they learn to understand themselves. They know which tone in a parent’s voice means trouble, when to stay quiet, when to step in and smooth things over. From the outside they look mature, dependable and wise beyond their years. But what goes unnoticed is the cost of a childhood spent managing others’ emotions.

This is parentification. Shristi Kharel is a psychologist with over six years of experience in psychological counseling, psychosocial support, and mental health training. She currently serves as a Mental Health Counselor and Trainer at Mankaa Kura.

Kharel discusses the patterns and the reason this tendency goes unnoticed, or even celebrated.

How can we understand parentification through the idea of development happening in a natural sequence?

Many people are familiar with Maslow’s hierarchy of needs, which suggests that before we can focus on growth, confidence, or reaching our full potential, our more basic needs—such as safety, security, and belonging—must first be adequately met. While real life is often more complex than a simple hierarchy, the idea reminds us that healthy development is built step by step.

In many ways, childhood follows a similar principle.

A child’s first developmental tasks are not to become the family’s peacemaker or emotional caregiver. They are to experience safety, love, protection, comfort, play, curiosity, and the freedom to express emotions. Through these experiences, children gradually develop trust, emotional regulation, confidence, and eventually responsibility.

Responsibility is not the problem. Responsibility that arrives before emotional security is.

What leads a child to assume the role of a parent?

In my clinical practice, I have rarely seen a child consciously choose this role. Rather, it develops gradually in response to the family environment.

Sometimes a parent is emotionally overwhelmed by conflict, loss, financial stress, mental health difficulties, or relationship problems. Without intending to, they begin relying on their child for emotional comfort, advice, or mediation.

A child may hear, "Talk to your father for me", "You're the only one who understands me” or "Don't tell anyone what's happening at home."

At first, these may seem like small requests. But repeated over months or years, they quietly reshape the child's identity. Instead of experiencing childhood as a time to receive care, the child learns that their role is to provide it.

Parentification is not created because children are unusually mature; it often develops because the adults around them are unable, for various reasons, to consistently carry the emotional responsibilities that belong to adulthood.

If attachment is supposed to be built on a child trusting that their needs will be met, what happens when the child learns that their job is to meet the parent's needs instead?

Healthy attachment teaches a child one fundamental belief: "When I am distressed, someone will comfort me."

Parentification reverses this belief.

The child begins to think, "When someone else is distressed, it is my responsibility to comfort them." Over time, their own emotional needs become less visible—not only to others, but to themselves. They may stop asking for help because they learn that needing care feels selfish or burdensome.

As adults, many of these individuals tell me, "I don't know how to receive love." They feel far more comfortable giving than receiving because childhood taught them that relationships are maintained by meeting other people's needs first.

What kind of attachment and emotional pattern does a child who is constantly managing a parent's moods develop?

There is no single attachment pattern that develops in every child, because every family is different. However, many children who grow up managing a parent's emotions develop anxious or fearful patterns of attachment.

Their nervous system becomes highly sensitive to emotional changes. They constantly scan people's expressions, voices, and behaviours, trying to predict what might happen next.

As adults, they become excellent at understanding other people's emotions while struggling to identify their own. They may fear conflict, avoid disappointing others, and believe that keeping relationships stable is entirely their responsibility.

One experience I repeatedly witness in therapy is that many parentified individuals can explain their childhood very well, but they struggle to describe how they actually felt.

When I ask, "How did you feel when your parents fought?" I often hear responses such as "They were under a lot of stress","I should understand them","They loved me."

These answers explain the parents' experience, but they often avoid the child's own emotional reality.

Over time, many children learn that their sadness, fear, anger, or disappointment might make an already struggling parent feel worse. So instead of expressing emotions, they suppress them. This emotional disconnection can continue well into adulthood.

Is there a kind of person we culturally celebrate, ‘the responsible eldest child' or the 'mature-beyond-their-years teenager', who may actually be a parentified child we have romanticised instead of supported?

Sometimes, yes.

Our culture often praises children who never complain, always help, never create problems, and seem unusually mature. These qualities can certainly reflect healthy development. However, as psychologists, we also ask another question: Did this maturity develop naturally, or was it necessary for survival?

I have met many adults who were praised throughout childhood for being ‘strong’. Yet, in therapy, they quietly admit they never felt they had permission to be scared, needy, or vulnerable.

The child we admire for being exceptionally responsible may sometimes be the child who learned far too early that there was no room for their own childhood.

If a parent is emotionally unpredictable (calm one moment and volatile the next) what does that unpredictability teach a child's nervous system?

Children learn about safety through repeated experiences.

When a parent's emotional responses are unpredictable, the child's nervous system learns that safety can disappear without warning. Many children become hypervigilant. They monitor every facial expression, every change in tone, every shift in mood.

This adaptation may help them survive childhood, but later in life it appears as anxiety, people-pleasing, overthinking, difficulty relaxing, or constantly expecting that something will go wrong. Their nervous system remains prepared for danger even when they are finally in safe relationships.

What does a parentified child often grow into? What might this look like in friendships, romantic relationships, or parenting?

Many parentified children become compassionate, dependable, and deeply caring adults. They are the friend everyone turns to, the partner who gives endlessly, the employee who carries everyone else's responsibilities, and the parent determined to never let their own children suffer.

These are genuine strengths.

Yet many also struggle to receive care themselves.

In therapy, I often hear statements like:

"I know my relationship isn't meeting my emotional needs, but I can't leave because I don't want to hurt them."

"I feel guilty whenever I say no."

"I don't know what I need anymore."

Their body may tell them that something feels wrong, while their mind insists that it is their responsibility to keep everyone else happy.

This inner conflict often traces back to childhood, when caring for others became more important than listening to themselves.

Can a parent be honest with a child about having a hard time without making it the child's burden?

Absolutely.

Children benefit from seeing that parents experience emotions. They do not need perfect parents—they need emotionally responsible ones.

There is a significant difference between saying, "I'm having a difficult day, but I'm taking care of it," and saying, "You're the only person who understands me. I don't know what I'd do without you."

The first teaches emotional openness with healthy boundaries.

The second unintentionally places adult emotional responsibility onto the child. Children can witness a parent's humanity without becoming responsible for carrying it.

If a parent recognises that they have been leaning on their child emotionally, what is the very first thing they should do differently?

The first step is not to become a perfect parent—it is to gently restore the natural direction of care.

Pause before asking your child to mediate conflicts, regulate your emotions, or become your confidant. Instead, seek emotional support from another adult—a partner, friend, family member, or mental health professional.

Then begin creating space for your child's emotional world.

Ask them, "How was your day?", "What are you feeling?", "Is there anything worrying you?"

And perhaps the most healing words a child can hear are these:

"You don't have to take care of me. I'm the adult. I'll take care of this. Your job is simply to be a child."

articles.title: How Nepal’s gym culture is growing beyond the young generation
articles.summary:
In recent years, the number of young people going to the gym has gone up significantly; this everyone knows. But it is not just a question of how many more people are working out, but also of who is working out. Gym-goers report a certain change in recent years in the weightlifting demographics.

It is not rare to see, during the late afternoon lull, retired folks on the treadmill or homemakers doing bicep curls and, in the evenings, to see 9-to-5 employees in their forties clocking into the gym after clocking out from work. What is behind this shift in the gym-goer demographic? Why are so many more uncles and aunties working out now?

“When I was growing up, people did not think of the gym the way they do now. Then, everyone in the gym seemed to already have massive backs and shoulders. When I told my mother I wanted to go to the gym, she told me it was a place for ruffians and extortionists. This is what people’s understanding was at the time, and it was true in ways; the gym was a place where a certain type of person could be found. This perception scared people. It made it unlikely that most would go [to the gym]," says Sunil Moktan, a powerlifter turned EREPS (European Register of Exercise Professionals)-certified trainer at Visionova Recreation.

It is not a surprise, then, that more everyday people were not crazy about getting that pump.

“The gym is seen as unsafe. People see these heavy weights, plates and rods and think that it's not a good idea to try to lift something so heavy. But training is, of course, controlled and gradual. The lack of correct information makes things hard for us trainers,” adds Rojen Shrestha, a former national dodgeball player turned powerlifter and trainer and is the other half of the two-man training operation at the gym.

“Social media definitely plays its part. Viewers see reels online of others working out. There are many fitness creators in Nepal pushing people to work out and explaining the benefits of doing so. That challenges traditional beliefs. It is not only Nepali creators. People have access to content from all over the world. Fitness content has always been big in the West, and as Nepali viewers see more of that, it changes who comes to workout,” Shrestha says.

Moktan adds, "Schools used to focus on education. That was the only thing that mattered – you had to study well. Now, most schools also focus on extracurricular activities and fitness as important things. If children come home with a certain idea, or if parents see what schools are focusing on, that helps to change people’s perceptions too.”

“Doctors are also to thank for the increase in older people going to the gym. Doctors will recommend their patients go to the gym to help them counteract loss of strength or if they have high cholesterol and other such things,” Moktan said.

“The gym is a preventive thing. It helps reduce the risk of health complications. Doctors will send patients to the gym if something goes wrong, but medical professionals should be telling people to start working out so things don’t get a chance to go wrong,” he also added.

There are still ways in which working out at the gym is seen in a negative light.

“Parents will tell their kids that so-and-so's kid went to the gym and got injured in such-and-such way, so you shouldn’t go. Another popular misconception is that working out at a young age will stop you from getting taller. There are many other misconceptions. It is not that everybody, suddenly, has adopted good sources of information. People have, but most have not,” Shrestha said.

People’s source of information repeatedly came up as the primary reason for the change in demographics but also the main problem in the industry.

“The gym has a lot of things that are new to a lot of people. For example, with diets, we recommend people eat a certain way so they can gain muscle. It is very common that our clients do not get enough protein. Clients do listen to us, but the people coming here are already better informed than most. It shows how well informed the average person might be,” Shrestha said.

“It is our part of our job as well to make sure people are well informed and understand what they are doing and why. But we alone cannot change everyone’s thinking. Other members of society whose voices are important need to also speak,” concludes Moktan smilingly.

articles.title: Australia tightens student visa rules, rejects 64 percent of Nepali applications
articles.summary:
Australia has rejected around 64 percent of offshore student visa applications from Nepal, marking the highest rejection rate recorded for Nepali applicants, according to official data.

The surge in visa refusals comes after the Australian government tightened its screening process for international students amid concerns over migration levels, housing pressures and the integrity of the education system.

Australia categorises countries under an “Evidence Level” risk framework to determine the level of scrutiny applied during visa processing. Education sector insiders say Nepal was recently moved to “Level 3”, the highest-risk category, from “Level 2” following a government review conducted several months ago.

The impact has been most severe in the vocational education and training (VET) sector, which traditionally attracts students seeking shorter and more affordable courses. Nearly 90 percent of Nepali applications for VET courses have been rejected, with only 56 of 549 applicants receiving visas, according to recent statistics.

Around 60,000 Nepali students are currently enrolled in Australian institutions. Of them, about 56,000 are existing students, while roughly 4,000 are new arrivals.

Data from Australia’s Department of Home Affairs shows a sharp decline in new student arrivals from Nepal. Between January and May this year, only 2,700 of 7,500 offshore applicants from Nepal were granted visas. During the same period last year, 7,167 of 8,028 applicants received approvals.

The uncertainty surrounding visa approvals, combined with rising application costs, has discouraged many prospective students. Applicants currently have to pay an application fee of A$2,500 (approximately Rs260,000), which is non-refundable even if the visa is rejected.

Sanjeev Pandey, a Sydney-based lawyer, said Australia had welcomed a large number of international students after the Covid-19 pandemic, but authorities later became concerned about patterns of students changing courses and extending their stay without completing their original programmes.

“The government may have also tightened student visa rules to address growing employment and housing pressures,” Pandey said.

The stricter visa regime has raised concerns among education consultancies and smaller institutions that rely heavily on international enrolments.

Khagendra Satyal, international business development manager at Central Australian College, said the decline in student arrivals had significantly affected the sector.

“Visas are now granted only after assessing what positive contributions an international student can make to Australia in the long run,” Satyal said. “Students applying from Nepal need to understand this shift.”

The immigration crackdown also comes amid growing political pressure in Australia over migration. Analysts say the rise of politicians with hardline positions on immigration, including Pauline Hanson, has contributed to a broader political push for tighter controls.

Lawyer Pandey said the tougher environment has affected not only prospective students but also those already in Australia. Renewing student visas, switching back to student visas after completing post-study work arrangements, and bringing spouses as dependants have all become more difficult, he said.

Obtaining permanent residency has also become significantly more challenging compared with previous years.

Despite the tightening measures, Nepal remains one of the largest sources of international students in Australia. Government data shows Nepali students account for around nine percent of Australia's international student population, making Nepal the third-largest source country.

articles.title: Budget-friendly places for Nepali students in Ohio
articles.summary:
Athens is a small, scenic college town in southeastern Ohio, shaped largely by Ohio University and its energetic student community. Surrounded by rolling hills, rivers and forests, the town combines historic streets, local businesses and easy access to nature.

The university campus, downtown shops and restaurants are concentrated within a compact area, making daily life manageable without a car. Ohio University students can also use Athens Public Transit free of charge, while nearby trails and forests provide inexpensive options for hiking and outdoor recreation.

Because Athens is a relatively small town, the number of professional internships available locally can be limited. Although Ohio University hosts career fairs and attracts employers from across the country, students may need to look beyond Athens or relocate temporarily for specialised opportunities.

Oxford is a compact, classic college town in southwestern Ohio, built almost entirely around Miami University at its core. Red-brick Georgian buildings, leafy streets and a walkable uptown give it a traditional campus-town character.

The compact layout means campus, uptown restaurants, shops and student housing are all within easy walking distance. The town is also considered quite safe, and Miami University's strong sense of community brings a steady calendar of campus events, traditions and activities that keep student life active without needing to travel elsewhere.

The town's economy is heavily tied to the university, so it can feel quiet or emptied out during breaks and summer months when students are away.

ColumbusColumbus is Ohio's capital and largest city, and it's where The Ohio State University, one of the biggest campuses in the country, is situated. Rather than a self-contained college town, Columbus functions as a full city with sprawling neighborhoods, a job market, and student population that's just one part of a much bigger urban picture.

Pros:Living costs stay reasonable even with everything a major city offers, and students get real exposure to internships and employers across finance, tech, healthcare and government without having to leave town.

Cons:The scale of the city brings more traffic and scattered housing options, so building a close community takes a bit more intention than it would in a smaller town.

Cincinnati is moving to universities like the University of Cincinnati and Xavier University. The city has 300,000 people and many residential areas.

Pros:The city offers people a diverse job market. It is home to many consumer goods, finance and healthcare companies. The cost of living is on the lower end for cities of this size.

Cons:Despite its universities, the city is not generally considered a college town. Younger residents have to actively seek college-town experiences since it is not part of city life. The city is also not walkable.

Toledo is Ohio’s fourth largest city, sitting on the edge of Lake Erie. It is a city of 600,000 people and home to the University of Toledo.

Pros: The University of Toledo sits at the centre of city life. It is the biggest school in town and also the town's biggest employer. Students have a solid pipeline to work experience and internships.

Cons: As a Rust Belt city, its growth has been stagnant over the years. And despite its size, it is considered to be falling behind the other major metros in Ohio.

Based on conversations with local Nepali students in Ohio.

articles.title: Migrant workers can strike under new Qatari labour law
articles.summary:
The Qatari government has introduced a conditional right for migrant workers to stage legal strikes as part of amendments to the country’s labour law.

Under the revised law, workers can go on strike for up to six working days after notifying their employer and the Ministry of Labour in writing, but only if a labour dispute cannot be resolved through negotiation, conciliation or mediation. The provision was introduced through Qatar’s Law No 9 of 2026, which amended the 2004 Labour Law (Law No 14) to strengthen workers’ rights and welfare.

The amended law requires companies with 100 or more employees to establish joint committees made up of management and worker representatives. The committees are intended to improve workplace dialogue, strengthen consultation and help resolve disputes before they escalate.

The reforms also introduce tougher penalties for labour violations. Employers that breach wage protection regulations may face suspension of ministry services, while the Labour Dispute Resolution Committee has been formally authorised to conduct virtual hearings. Recruitment agencies and companies involved in hiring violations may face fines ranging from QAR3,000 to QAR25,000. One Qatari riyal is equivalent to Rs41.66.

Workers exercising their right to strike will not be entitled to wages during the strike period. The law also allows companies to dismiss without notice workers who organise illegal or unjustified strikes without following the required procedures or who disrupt business operations through such actions.

Companies that fail to establish mandatory joint committees may face fines ranging from QAR2,000 to QAR5,000.

Qatar has also strengthened enforcement of its Wage Protection System. The amended law gives the labour ministry greater authority to take action against employers that delay or fail to pay salaries, including suspending services, imposing administrative measures and applying regulatory penalties against repeat offenders.

If a company repeatedly violates wage rules or triggers collective disputes because of unpaid salaries, other companies under the same ownership may also face penalties. The ministry may publish the names of non-compliant companies on its website.

Workers who remain unpaid can request a change of employer or terminate their contracts, with repatriation costs to be covered by the employer.

The Labour Dispute Resolution Committee’s new authority to conduct virtual hearings means workers no longer need to be physically present to pursue labour cases. Employers, workers and verified witnesses can now participate in proceedings online.

Workers must first register disputes with the ministry. Cases are referred to the dispute resolution committee only when efforts to settle them through negotiation fail. Agreements reached through ministry-led mediation will have the status of legally enforceable documents.

The amended law also increases penalties for recruitment-related violations.

Recruitment agencies can be fined between QAR3,000 and QAR25,000 for hiring workers without ministry approval for employment contracts, processing recruitment before mandatory medical examinations or committing other administrative and recruitment-related violations.

Qatari recruitment agencies generally recruit workers in partnership with manpower agencies in Nepal, although some employers also hire directly through Nepali firms.

The new rules also require workers seeking employment in designated technical and professional occupations to obtain certificates confirming that they have completed required training and passed examinations at ministry-approved centres before starting work.

Meanwhile, Qatar has extended the non-compete period, during which an employee can be restricted from joining a competing company after leaving a job, from one year to two years. The change restores a provision that existed before 2020.

If an employee has access to sensitive client information, trade secrets or confidential company data, an employer can prevent them from joining a competitor for up to two years after the termination of employment.

The labour law amendments are aimed at modernising Qatar’s labour market, improving regulatory oversight and creating a more flexible and competitive employment system in line with the Qatar National Vision 2030. Some provisions will require additional decrees and executive regulations before they come into full effect.

“These reforms represent significant shifts that will heavily impact employers, workers, recruitment agencies and the dispute resolution system alike,” Krishna Panthi, president of the Non-Resident Nepali Association Qatar, told Kantipur.

articles.title: 67 Nepalis died in Japan over ten months, 25 killed themselves
articles.summary:
As many as 67 Nepali citizens have died in Japan over the past ten months, including 25 suicides, according to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. Most of the deceased were individuals who had travelled on student visas and were also working part-time.

The deaths were recorded between mid-July, 2025 and June 1, 2026. While some cases list medical or other causes, many certificates state the reason as “unknown”. Illness-related deaths remain relatively low, officials said.

Acting Nepali ambassador to Japan Harihar Kant Poudel said the rising number of deaths has made body management increasingly difficult. “In some cases, families perform the funeral rites in Japan. In others, the embassy is not informed even after cremation,” he said.

Repatriating a body from Japan to Nepal costs around Rs1.2 million. Educational institutions sending students abroad on student visas are not covering these expenses and are often not in contact with the embassy.

Many students arriving for language studies on student visas have been taking up work. However, they are not required to obtain labour permits from the Department of Foreign Employment. As a result, the Foreign Employment Board does not provide financial assistance for repatriation or related support when deaths occur outside the formal labour system.

Deaths and suicides have been reported mainly among workers in construction, Nepal-run hotels and restaurants, and supply companies. Around 6,000 Nepal-operated hotels and restaurants are estimated to be running in Japan, where labour protections such as health insurance and social security are not consistently ensured.

Education consultancies in Nepal have been sending students to Japan by charging high fees and making what critics describe as misleading promises. Japanese government data shows that by 2025, around 116,000 Nepali students were living in Japan, making Nepal the second-largest source of foreign students after China. Overall, Nepalis are the fifth-largest migrant group in Japan, with a total population of about 309,000, including 9,908 permanent residents.

According to the Non-Resident Nepali Association Japan, many students are under severe financial and psychological pressure due to high-interest loans taken in Nepal.

“Living costs in Japan are high, and earnings from 28 working hours a week are not enough for rent, food and tuition,” said NRNA Japan secretary Sachin Acharya. “When families in Nepal demand loan repayments, it adds mental stress. Switching from student visas to work visas requires language proficiency and other conditions, which are difficult. This is contributing to rising suicides.”

He said many students come on student visas due to easier access, but struggle to find stable work. “Some have to rely on money from Nepal. Many Nepalis are being arrested for exceeding the 28-hour work limit,” he said. “The Nepali embassy is understaffed, which makes it difficult to handle prison visits and related cases.”

Nepali student Uma Khatri, currently in Japan, said the reality is far more difficult than expected. “You need strong Japanese language skills before coming here. It is manageable for those who can work hard, but very difficult for students,” she said. “City living is expensive. Rural areas are cheaper, but jobs are scarce. Attendance requirements are strict, and visa renewal can be affected.”

Hira Shrestha from Baglung, who paid Rs1.35 million to reach Japan, said even working beyond permitted hours does not ease financial pressure. “People expect to repay loans quickly, but many struggle for years,” he said. Survival itself is hard.”

He said consultancy firms often present an overly optimistic picture. “They say you can study language for a year and work, but there is no job guarantee. Competition for part-time work is intense,” he said. “Some take multiple jobs to save money, which is illegal and can lead to visa cancellation.”

Only a small number of Nepalis go to Japan as skilled workers, while many enter as trainees in the agriculture and business sectors. The Nepali embassy has urged authorities to avoid sending workers under individual labour permits through the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and labour channels.

In the last fiscal year, 18,744 Nepalis received labour approval from the Department of Foreign Employment, including both institutional and individual permits, with 5,800 women among them.

The embassy said it mainly tracks trainee workers sent through approved channels, where employers or agencies can be held responsible in case of death, making repatriation easier. However, it lacks records of students and individuals who arrive outside formal labour approval systems, complicating assistance and monitoring.

articles.title: पोखरीमा डुबेर भारतीय दर्शनार्थीको मृत्यु
articles.summary:
जनकपुरधामस्थित जानकी मन्दिरको छेउमा रहेको तेल्हा पोखरीमा डुबेर गए राति एक भारतीय दर्शनार्थीको मृत्यु भएको छ।

साथीहरूसँग जानकी मन्दिर दर्शन गर्न आएका भारतको विहार राज्यको हाजीरपुर निवासी २० वर्षीय आदर्शकुमार झाले अचानक पोखरीमा डुबेर मृत्यु भएको जिल्ला प्रहरी कार्यालय धनुषाका प्रवक्ता प्रहरी नायब उपरीक्षक मधुसुदन न्यौपानेले जानकारी दिए।

पोखरीमा हामफालेपछि स्थानीय युवाहरूले तत्काल उनको उद्धार गरी उपचारका लागि जनकपुरधामस्थित प्रादेशिक अस्पतालमा भर्ना गरिएकामा उपचारका क्रममा मृत्यु भएको प्रहरी नायब उपरीक्षक न्यौपानेले बताए।

शव परीक्षणका लागि अस्पतालमा राखिएको र घटनाबारे थप अनुसन्धान भइरहेको प्रहरी नायब उपरीक्षक न्यौपानेको भनाइ छ।

articles.title: हाइब्रिड राष्ट्रवाद र राजनीतिक अन्योल
articles.summary:
इतिहास साक्षी छ, जब–जब कुनै समाजले आफ्नो आन्तरिक स्वाभिमान र रैथाने चिन्तनको धरातल गुमाउँछ, तब त्यसको मानसिक संकट लुकाउन ‘उग्र र प्रदर्शनकारी देशभक्ति’को जन्म हुन्छ। त्यसले एकप्रकारले अन्योलता वा द्विविधा उत्पन्न गराउँदै जान्छ। त्यही प्रसंगसँग मेल खाने विचार इटालेली चिन्तक एन्टोनियो ग्राम्सीले ‘शासक वर्गले आफ्नो शक्ति जोगाउन समाजमा एउटा यस्तो झुटो चेतना पैदा गरिदिन्छ, जहाँ सर्वसाधारण नागरिक आफ्ना वास्तविक समस्या बिर्सेर सत्ताकै स्वार्थलाई आफ्नो भाग्य ठान्न पुग्छन्।’

फ्रान्ज फ्याननले यसलाई अझ स्पष्ट पार्दै लेखेका छन्– ‘तेस्रो विश्वका बुद्धिजीवीहरू बाहिर जतिसुकै उग्र राष्ट्रवादको नारा लगाए पनि भित्रभित्रै पश्चिमा मालिकहरूको विकृत अनुकरण र गुलामी गरिरहेका हुन्छन्।’

यस्तै विरोधाभासलाई समात्दै अर्का विद्वान् थिओडोर एडोर्नोले चेतावनी दिएका थिए कि आधुनिक युगको राष्ट्रवाद कुनै आत्मिक विवेक होइन, बरु बजार र सत्ताले आफ्नो स्वार्थका लागि नागरिकलाई अल्झाउन तयार पारेको एउटा ‘देखावटी भावुकता’ मात्र हो।’

यिनै झुटो चेतना, मानसिक गुलामी र देखावटी भावुकताको आधुनिक रूपलाई नै ‘हाइब्रिड राष्ट्रवाद’ भनिन्छ। त्यसलाई नेपालीमा वर्णशंकर राष्ट्रवाद हुन्छ।संसारमा कुनै पनि मानव सभ्यता, भाषा, संस्कार–संस्कृति र विचारहरू निरपेक्ष वा शुद्ध हुँदैनन्। ऐतिहासिक आदानप्रदानको क्रममा यिनीहरू कुनै न कुनै रूप एकअन्तर भई वर्णशंकर बनेकै हुन्छन्। सभ्यताको विकासक्रममा यस्तो विचार वा संस्कृतिको शंकरणले समाजलाई गतिशील र रूपान्तरणकारी बनाउन कति योगदान दियो भन्ने कुरा नै महत्त्वपूर्ण पाटो हो तर समकालीन नेपालको सन्दर्भमा भने यस्तो वर्णशंकर विचार वा राष्ट्रवादले समाजलाई कुनै सकारात्मक रूपान्तरण र निकास दिनुको सट्टा झन् उग्र, छद्म र अन्योलग्रस्त बनाएको छ।

यस परिप्रेक्ष्यमा ग्राम्सीले भनेको झुटो चेतना, फ्याननले औंल्याएको मानसिक गुलामी र एडोर्नोले देखाएको नक्कली भावुकताको कसीमा उभिएर अनि ‘सायारेम्मा’ले निर्देश गरेको मुन्दुमी स्वाभिमानको ऐना हेरेर आजको यो खोक्रो हाइब्रिड राष्ट्रवादको मनोवैज्ञानिक एवं दार्शनिक शल्यक्रिया गर्नु अपरिहार्य भइसकेको छ। त्यसैले यहाँ क्रमशः इतिहासको विद्रोही चेत, वर्तमानको वैचारिक परनिर्भरतालगायत वर्णशंकर, राजनीतिक विचार सिद्धान्त र आयामहरूलाई समेट्दै, नेपाली बौद्धिक वृत्त र युवा मानसमा जरो गाड्दै गएको हाइब्रिडराष्ट्रवादी भ्रमको मुकुण्डो उतार्ने र वास्तविक, स्वाभिमानी राष्ट्रप्रेमतर्फको यात्रालाई पुनर्जीवित गर्ने प्राज्ञिक प्रयास गरिएको छ।

मेरो पूर्ववर्ती पुस्तक ‘सायारेम्मा: राष्ट्रवाद कि राष्ट्रप्रेम’मा मीमांसा गरिएझैं सायारेम्मा भनेको मानिसको भित्री शीर उठाउने र रैथाने स्वाभिमान जागृत गराउने कुरा, जुन सात्विक राष्ट्रप्रेमको शाश्वत धरातल र विविध राष्ट्रियताहरूको संयुक्त विचारधारा राष्ट्रवादको अर्गानिक स्वरूप हो।

हाइब्रिड राष्ट्रवाद बहस: हाइब्रिड राष्ट्रवादको वकालत गर्नेहरू एउटा कुनामा मात्र छैनन्, उनीहरू राष्ट्रका प्रायः सबै स्थानमा ह्वात्तै बढिरहेका छन्। दिन दुई गुणा रात चौगुणा बढिरहेको हाइब्रिड राष्ट्रवादीहरू बाहिर प्रगतिशील र क्रान्तिकारी देखिने शीर्ष राजनीतिक नेतृत्वदेखि लिएर, कुनै विचारबिनाको उग्र नारा बेच्ने नयाँ ‘पपुलिस्टहरू’ र पश्चिमा फन्डिङमा हुर्किएका सुकिला थिंक–ट्यांकका ‘बौद्धिक दलाल’हरू सबैको विचार आज एउटै बिन्दुमा छन्। दक्षिणपन्थी संकीर्णता र वैचारिक आत्मसमर्पणजस्ता पश्चगामी विचारबाट ग्रसित, दृश्य–अदृश्य पात्रहरू संघीय लोकतान्त्रिक गणतन्त्रलाई वास्तविक रूपमा संस्थागत गर्ने मुद्दाहरूलाई ओझेलमा र आफ्नो असफलता लुकाउन जनतालाई खोक्रो र कृत्रिम राष्ट्रवादको अफिम खुवाइरहेका छन्।

आजको दिनसम्म आइपुग्दा राजनीतिक र प्राज्ञिक परिदृश्यमा ‘हाइब्रिड राष्ट्रवादी विचार’को वकालत कुनै एउटा व्यक्ति वा दलले मात्र गरेका छैनन्, विभिन्न शक्ति, समूह र पात्रहरूको एउटा अनौठो गठजोडबाट सञ्चालित छ, जहाँ सबैको राजनीतिक र वैचारिक पृष्ठभूमि फरक–फरक छन् तर पनि भित्रभित्रै उनीहरूको चरित्र एउटै छ। बाहिर प्रगतिशील/उग्र नारा, भित्र दक्षिणपन्थी अजेन्डा र वैचारिक परनिर्भरता।

त्यसो हुनाले नेपालको सन्दर्भमा यो हाइब्रिड राष्ट्रवादको वकालत सैदान्तिक रूपमा कसले गर्छ र कसले मलजल गर्छ भन्ने मूलतः चार प्रमुख पात्र/समूहमा वर्गीकरण गरी चिरफार गर्‍यो भने बुझ्न अझै सहज हुनेछ।

पहिलो कुरा उनीहरू प्रगतिशील मुकुण्डोधारी राजनीतिक नेतृत्व गरिरहेका हुन्छन्। नेपालमा हाइब्रिड राष्ट्रवादका सबैभन्दा ठुला वाहक स्थापित ठुला दल कम्युनिस्ट र समाजवादी/प्रजातान्त्रिक पार्टी र शीर्ष नेताहरू नै छन्। उनीहरूको चरित्र बाहिर समाजवाद, संघीयता, समावेशिता र साम्राज्यवाद–विरोधी चर्का भाषण दिन्छन् तर व्यवहारमा उनीहरूको विचार पूरै दक्षिणपन्थी, पश्चगामी र वैदेशिक शक्तिहरूसँगको गुप्त सम्झौतामा आधारित हुन्छ। विशेषतः उनीहरूको चरित्र भाषण र व्यवहारमा विरोधाभासपूर्ण देखिन्छ। उनीहरू सडक र चुनावी सभाहरूमा ‘राष्ट्रिय स्वाभिमान’को उग्र नारा उराल्दै बेच्ने तर सत्तामा पुगेपछि राज्यका स्रोतसाधन शक्ति राष्ट्रहरूको पुँजीपतिहरूलाई बुझाउने र भूराजनीतिक शक्तिहरूसँग आत्मसमर्पण गर्ने दोहोरो चरित्र नै उनीहरूको हाइब्रिड रूप हो।

यति मात्र होइन, उनीहरूबाहेकका उदाइरहेका नयाँ शक्ति नयाँ ‘लोकप्रियतावादी’ र भर्चुअल भिडका अगुवाहरू पनि हाइब्रिड राष्ट्रवादी हुन्। उनीहरूको चरित्र प्रणालीको विरोध गरेझैं गर्छन् र कुनै वैचारिक धरातल वा दर्शनबिनाको ‘विशुद्ध देशभक्ति’को नारा दिन्छन्। उनीहरूसँग संघीय गणतन्त्रलाई सुदृढ बनाउने वा देशको वर्गीय संकट हल गर्ने कुनै स्पष्ट राजनीतिक–आर्थिक मार्गचित्र छैन। त्यो पक्षमा खासै अगाडि बढ्न चाहँदैनन्। उनीहरूले फैलाउने राष्ट्रवाद केवल सतही, भर्चुअल आक्रोश र दक्षिणपन्थी संकीर्णता (जात, धर्म वा कृत्रिम शत्रु) मा आधारित हुन्छ। त्यसैगरी तेस्रो आधार भनेको ‘प्रोजेक्टेड’ बुद्धिजीवी र दाता–पोषित थिंक–ट्यांकहरू पनि हाइब्रिड राष्ट्रवादीहरू हुन्। उनीहरू नेपालका प्रमुख विश्वविद्यालय, काठमाडौंका ‘सुकिला–मुकिला’ अध्ययन संस्थान थिंक थ्यांक र विदेशी अनुदान संस्थाहरूमा आधारित प्राज्ञिक दलाल र विश्लेषकहरू आदि पर्छन्। मूलतः उनीहरूको चरित्र आफूलाई स्वतन्त्र, नागरिक समाज वा भू–राजनीतिक विज्ञका रूपमा प्रस्तुत गर्छन्। तर उनीहरूको विचार र व्यवहारमा यथेष्ट विरोधाभास हुन्छन्। उनीहरू प्रायः पश्चिमा ज्ञानका कारखाना वा बाह्य दातृ निकायबाट उत्पादित भाष्यहरूलाई नेपाली माटोमा राष्ट्रिय हितको लेबल लगाएर आयात गरिरहेका हुन्छन्। बाहिर रैथाने वा समावेशी कुरा गर्ने तर भित्रभित्रै नेपालको रैथाने दर्शन सायारेम्मा र मौलिक आलोचनात्मक चेतलाई ध्वस्त पार्ने काम उनीहरूबाटै गराइरहेका हुन्छन्।

त्यसैगरी अर्को आधार भनेको दक्षिणपन्थी–संरक्षक मिडिया र डिजिटल इको–चेम्बर मुख्यधारका कर्पोरेट मिडिया हाउसहरू र सामाजिक सञ्जालका संगठित ‘ट्रोल’ वा ‘पेज’ सञ्चालकहरू। मूलतः उनीहरू राष्ट्रवादलाई एउटा बिक्री हुने सामग्री बनाउँछन्। जस्तै देशमा भ्रष्टाचार, संघीयताको निष्प्रभाविता वा नीतिगत टाटपल्टाइमाथि प्रश्न उठ्नेबित्तिकै उनीहरूले कुनै उग्र भावनात्मक वा दक्षिणपन्थी मुद्दा उछालेर जनताको ध्यान मोड्न उद्दत हुन्छन्। दक्षिणपन्थी संरक्षकहरूले नै सत्य बोल्ने अर्गानिक बुद्धिजीवीहरूलाई देशद्रोहीको बिल्ला भिराउने काम गर्छन्।

हाम्रो यथार्थ: हाम्रो समाजको मौलिक धरातल पूरै खण्डित कर्म अन्त्य हुनुपर्ने र स्वतःस्फुर्ट राष्ट्रप्रेम र राष्ट्रवादी भावनाले उद्देलित हुनुपर्ने थियो तर वर्तमान राजनीतिको विरूप यो व्यवस्थाले संस्थागत आकार लिन नपाउँदै हाइब्रिड राष्ट्रवादको चपेटामा परेर अन्योलता र दिशाहीनको बाटोमा पुग्यो। दलहरू उनीहरूको आदर्श र ऐतिहासिक अजेन्डाहरूबाट पूरै च्युत भई नीतिगत रूपमा शून्यमा प्रायः हुनुपुग्यो। बाहिरी लेपबाट हेर्दा यो व्यवस्था बलियो र स्थिरजस्तो देखिए पनि भित्रभित्रै दलहरू भित्रको वैचारिक परनिर्भरता र शक्ति संघर्षले गर्दा संघीयताको जग नै हल्लिएको छ। यो छद्म राष्ट्रवादी होहल्लाले व्यवस्थाका वास्तविक चुनौतीहरूजस्तै प्रदेशहरूको स्वायत्तता, साधन–स्रोतको न्यायिक बाँडफाँड र संवैधानिक निकायहरूको निष्पक्षतामाथि हुनुपर्ने गम्भीर राजनीतिक विमर्शहरू पूरै ओझेलमा परेको छ। जसले समग्र गणतान्त्रिक पद्धतिलाई नै एउटा अकल्पनीय अन्योलको भुमरीमा धकेलिदिएको अवस्था छ। संसद् जनताको निम्ति नीति निर्माणको थलो हुनुको सट्टा क्षणिक चुनावी दाउपेच र दक्षिणपन्थी विचारसँगको गुप्त लेनदेनको अखडा बन्न पुग्यो। यी कमजोरीले गर्दा समग्र गणतान्त्रिक पद्धतिमाथि नै आमनागरिकको अनास्था तीव्र रूपमा बढ्दै गयो।

यसरी एकातिर राज्यको संघीय संरचना चरम नीतिगत शून्यताबाट गुज्रिनु र अर्कातिर प्रगतिशील भनिएका शक्तिहरूको विचार पूरै दक्षिणपन्थी अजेन्डासँग मिल्न जानुले नेपाली राजनीतिलाई कतै नभेटिने अँध्यारो सुरुङनजिकै पु¥याएको छ र समग्र व्यवस्था नै कुनै पनि बेला दुर्घटनामा पर्न सक्ने गम्भीर खतरा पैदा भएको छ।

articles.title: सिरहाको लहानमा पेस्तोलसहित तीन जना पक्राउ
articles.summary:
सिरहाको लहान नगरपालिका वडा नम्बर २२ सलोखरीबाट प्रहरीले म्याग्जिन सहितको पेस्तोल बरामद गर्दै तीन जनालाई पक्राउ गरेको छ।

प्रहरी चौकी सितापुरबाट खटिएको गस्ती टोलीले शंकास्पद रूपमा हिँडिरहेका सबरजीत दासलाई चेकजाँच गर्ने क्रममा उनको साथबाट ९ एमएम जस्तो देखिने म्याग्जिनसहितको पुरानो पेस्तोल बरामद गरेको प्रहरीले जनाएको छ।

घटनामा संलग्न रहेको आरोपमा गुरुदेव दास र संजय दासलाई समेत नियन्त्रणमा लिइएको प्रहरीले जनाएको छ। पक्राउ परेका तीनै जनामाथी थप अनुसन्धान भइरहेको इलाका प्रहरी कार्यालय लहानले जनाएको छ।

articles.title: सिमलतालमा पहिरो खस्दा नारायणगढ-मुग्लिन सडक अवरुद्ध
articles.summary:
चितवनको सिमलताल नजिकै लेदोसहितको पहिरो खस्दा नारायणगढ-मुग्लिन सडक खण्ड पूर्णरूपमा अवरुद्ध भएको छ।

बुधबार बिहान ७:०५ बजे उक्त सडक खण्डको सिमलताल नजिक (किलोमिटर २४+६५०) पहिरो खस्दा आवागमन दुईतर्फी नै बन्द भएको हो। सडक डिभिजन भरतपुरका अनुसार पहिरो हटाउनका लागि अहिले सडक डिभिजनको उपकरण परिचालन भइसकेको छ।

पहिरो पन्छाएर सडक आवागमन पूर्णरूपमा सञ्चालनमा ल्याउने तयारी भइरहेको छ।

articles.title: पोखरीमा डुबेर भारतीय दर्शनार्थीको मृत्यु
articles.summary:
जनकपुरधामस्थित जानकी मन्दिरको छेउमा रहेको तेल्हा पोखरीमा डुबेर गए राति एक भारतीय दर्शनार्थीको मृत्यु भएको छ।

साथीहरूसँग जानकी मन्दिर दर्शन गर्न आएका भारतको विहार राज्यको हाजीरपुर निवासी २० वर्षीय आदर्शकुमार झाले अचानक पोखरीमा डुबेर मृत्यु भएको जिल्ला प्रहरी कार्यालय धनुषाका प्रवक्ता प्रहरी नायब उपरीक्षक मधुसुदन न्यौपानेले जानकारी दिए।

पोखरीमा हामफालेपछि स्थानीय युवाहरूले तत्काल उनको उद्धार गरी उपचारका लागि जनकपुरधामस्थित प्रादेशिक अस्पतालमा भर्ना गरिएकामा उपचारका क्रममा मृत्यु भएको प्रहरी नायब उपरीक्षक न्यौपानेले बताए।

शव परीक्षणका लागि अस्पतालमा राखिएको र घटनाबारे थप अनुसन्धान भइरहेको प्रहरी नायब उपरीक्षक न्यौपानेको भनाइ छ।

articles.title: Shashank Koirala set to spearhead split in Nepali Congress
articles.summary:
Shashank Koirala may have harboured the ambition of leading the Nepali Congress as its president, but the former general secretary now stands at a historic crossroads. He is preparing to lead a prospective new political outfit outside the traditional four-starred banner and election symbol “tree”.

Following opposition from the Sher Bahadur Deuba-led faction to the Congress’s special general convention held earlier this year, the group is organising a three-day national gathering in Kathmandu from August 14 to 16. It will prepare for the formation of a separate political party, unless a dramatic reconciliation occurs between the Congress factions anytime soon.

When the former acting president Purna Bahadur Khadka stepped back from coordinating the event, the Deuba faction appointed Koirala on Saturday to steer the 521-member main organising committee. Until then, Khadka had been heading the activities of the Deuba faction.

On Saturday, Shashank not only replaced Khadka but also took on the leadership role with a firm commitment to spearheading a new party—minus the tree symbol and the four-starred flag.

“Shashank Koirala is our leader today, and he will remain our leader moving forward,” said senior party leader Bimalendra Nidhi.

The day after his appointment, Shashank hosted the first top-level strategic meeting at his residence in Maharajgunj on Sunday. However, his decision has drawn sharp criticism across social media platforms, with many accusing the son of the legendary founder BP Koirala, of engineering a party split. Public sentiment remains largely hostile to the move.

Muktinath Panta, a former security supervisor currently employed at the Smithsonian Institution’s National Air and Space Museum, expressed deep dismay over Shashank’s decision on Facebook. “My goodness, what has happened to the intellect of BP’s son? Where will following leaders like Mohan Bahadur Basnet, Min Bishwakarma, Kanchharam Tamang, and Kundan Raj Kafle lead him after breaking the party? Destruction leads to perverted wisdom. What would BP think from above? He could have at least remained inactive. After enjoying power for so many years on his father’s legacy, he is now choosing to sink the ship along with himself.”

Tej Bahadur Raut, a former teacher currently residing in South Korea, wrote, “He [Shashank] neither possesses the capacity to establish a party nor the ability to run one successfully.

“Nor did he accomplish anything significant while remaining within the Nepali Congress. He has no proven capability other than receiving things served on a platter.”

Addressing Shashank directly, former senator of Tribhuvan University Pankaj Subedi posted, “Personally, Dr Shashank Koirala is a good man. I remain hopeful that he will act in the broader interest of the Nepali Congress. Please engage in restrained and constructive discussions with President Gagan Thapa to build a unified Nepali Congress. Do not allow this conspiracy to stain your legacy permanently.”

Although a few supporters attempted to defend his move, such positive responses were heavily outnumbered on social media.

Prior to entering full-time politics, both Shashank Koirala and his cousin Shekhar Koirala worked in the medical profession. Shashank established his reputation as an ophthalmologist, while Shekhar practised as a physician. Both transitioned into active politics primarily to assist the late party president Girija Prasad Koirala. Their entry into central-level politics came formally during the party’s 11th general convention in 2006.

During that convention, Shashank was elected as a central working committee member when only 25 seats were open for election, securing the highest number of votes after Sushil Koirala. In contrast, Shekhar was nominated to the committee directly by Girija Prasad Koirala.

At the 13th general convention in 2016, Shashank was elected general secretary with minimal campaign effort. During that election, he defeated Gagan Thapa, who now serves as the party president. Another prominent leader, Arjun Narsingh KC was also in the contest. Yet, Shashank did not even need to actively solicit votes from the delegates. At the time, he was viewed across the party rank and file as the physical living shadow of BP. The heavy political legacy of the Koirala family, paired with emotional appeal and widespread trust among cadres, positioned him as the natural successor for the party presidency. However, during his five-year tenure as general secretary, he failed to translate that organisational capital into active leadership.

Shashank was rarely seen taking a proactive role in party organisation, refrained from driving ideological debates, and remained largely silent in parliament. As his term progressed, he gradually transitioned from a decisive figure into an inactive politician. Although he held strong ambitions to run for party president at the 14th general convention, neither the establishment faction showed interest in backing him nor did the opposition faction place its ultimate trust in him. The establishment re-nominated Sher Bahadur Deuba, while the opposition group put forward Shekhar.

Even when his own cousin Shekhar ran for the post, Shashank refrained from openly endorsing him. Instead, his close proximity to Deuba drew severe criticism from within the opposition camp. Consequently, he was completely left out of the presidential race he wished to contest.

Having spent over four decades in Nepali Congress politics and enjoying a natural stature as the youngest son of BP Koirala, Shashank now stands at a decisive juncture. Once expected to lead the entire Nepali Congress by carrying forward BP’s legacy, he has chosen a path that strays from the political tradition founded by his own father.

How Shashank agreed to lead the breakaway faction

Until Friday, the question of who would assume the leadership remained unresolved even within the Deuba faction. According to a senior leader from the Deuba camp, Khadka maintained a firm stance against leading a party split from the outset, which excluded his name from serious consideration.

Consequently, attention shifted entirely toward the Koirala brothers. Leaders within the faction noted that a majority agreed to project Shekhar if he was willing to accept the role.

Sources revealed that a high-level meeting involving leaders Bimalendra Nidhi, Krishna Prasad Sitaula, Prakash Man Singh, Prakash Sharan Mahat, NP Saud, and Bijay Kumar Gachhadar took place on Friday to settle the leadership issue. The key turning point occurred when Shekhar, who was in Biratnagar on Friday, telephoned Sitaula and proposed projecting Shashank instead, signalling his own reluctance to head a breakaway faction.

Following Shekhar’s retreat, the meeting turned to Shashank as the primary choice. Before reaching a final decision, leaders posed a direct question to him: “Are you ready to lead not just the national gathering on August 14, but all subsequent political processes that follow?” When Shashank explicitly replied “I am ready,” the committee formally put his name forward.

Unless dramatic political developments unfold within the next two weeks, Shashank is set to become the president of a newly registered party, officially separating from the mainstream Nepali Congress.

Among BP Koirala’s three sons, the eldest Prakash, and Shashank were active in politics. Following King Gyanendra’s takeover in 2005, Prakash joined the royal cabinet as the minister for environment, science, and technology.

Due to his support for the royal move, the Nepali Congress expelled Prakash even from ordinary party membership. Since the collapse of the King’s direct rule, Prakash has been unable to return to Congress politics and has largely vanished from the national scene.

Following Prakash’s exit from the mainstream, Girija brought Shekhar and Shashank into central politics together to establish an institutional line of succession within the Koirala family. Now, following Prakash’s footsteps, Shashank is also prepared to abandon the party founded by his father.

When asked how he views the departure of both sons of BP from the party mainstream, Prakash said, “I could not remain active in the Nepali Congress mainly because of the governance style observed over the past 10 to 15 years and the party’s decision to abolish the constitutional monarchy. The core issue was that I disapproved of the political parties’ governance style following the royal palace massacre.”

Prakash further claimed that Girija never intended to make him the political heir. “Had that been the case, why would I have reached the point of leaving the party?”

However, Gokarna Paudel, a senior party leader who spent 20 years as an aide to Girija, clarified that the original line of succession was never centered on BP’s sons, but rather on the trio known colloquially as ‘RSS’—Ramchandra Poudel, Shailaja Acharya, and Sher Bahadur Deuba.

In the initial years, Deuba was the primary favourite. Later, Girija shifted his preference to Ramchandra. As trust eroded with Poudel as well, Sushil Koirala emerged as the key successor. “It was only after Sushil came to prominence that a desire to promote Shashank over Shekhar became apparent,” said Paudel.

“Sushil and Shashank were uncle and nephew. During their years in exile, they shared a room and maintained a close personal bond. That is why Sushil favoured Shashank over Shekhar,” said Paudel. “Sushil’s true wish was to see Shashank become the president of the party. Now, it appears he may get the opportunity to become the president of one faction, if not the entire Nepali Congress.”

Meanwhile, Prakash Koirala argues that establishing a new party from within the Nepali Congress holds no practical utility in contemporary politics, criticising his younger brother’s decision as ill-advised.

“He has taken a decision out of confusion and frustration. One must exercise patience in politics. BP Koirala exercised immense patience, which ultimately saved the nation and ushered in democracy. That historical lesson must not be forgotten,” said Prakash. “Now is not the time to form a new party. There are already numerous political groups operating in BP’s name. The goal should be to bring everyone together under one roof, rather than plunging the country into further chaos.”

Defending his decision, Shashank stated that circumstances forced him onto this path. “Despite our continuous efforts, patience, and initiatives to maintain complete unity within the party, leaders in executive positions failed to play a meaningful role. Therefore, we were compelled to organise this national gathering to address the deep disappointment prevailing among party leaders, cadres, elected representatives, supporters, and well-wishers,” said Shashank, addressing a press conference on Saturday after assuming the coordinator's role.

Party insiders say that these developments are happening with the full knowledge of former president Deuba. However, it remains uncertain whether Deuba himself will actively participate in the national gathering or the formal registration of a new party.

Deuba’s own actions contributed significantly to the internal rift. On April 17, the Supreme Court upheld the Election Commission’s decision to recognise the special general convention and the central working committee headed by Thapa. Unsatisfied with the verdict, the Deuba faction filed a review petition with the court.

Unless a dramatic turn of events unfolds prior to the gathering, the registration of a new party remains nearly certain. Leaders aligned with the Deuba faction indicated that the new party will be officially announced during the closed-door session following the inauguration of the national gathering on August 14.

Although the name of the new party has not been decided, internal discussions on it are ongoing. Sitaula has proposed naming it the ‘Nepali Congress (Muldhar)’, while Nidhi suggested “Progressive Congress”. Other leaders have argued for the 'Nepali National Congress' to connect the entity with its historical legacy. Nidhi stated that all operational guidelines and party directions will be finalised at the upcoming gathering.

articles.title: Four and a half months on, Shah government faces questions over governance
articles.summary:
Four and a half months after Prime Minister Balendra Shah took office, his government finds itself facing mounting criticism over its style of governance, with opponents, constitutional experts and political analysts accusing it of sidelining democratic institutions while pursuing rapid reforms.

Since assuming office on March 27, the government has presented itself as an administration determined to overhaul Nepal’s governance system through swift structural changes. But many of its major decisions over the past 130 days have sparked controversy, prompting questions about transparency, accountability and adherence to constitutional procedures.

Critics say the government has increasingly relied on social media to communicate major policy decisions, often creating confusion over official processes. The prime minister’s Facebook posts have regularly featured policy announcements, political commentary and responses to controversies, leading opponents to accuse him of attempting to govern through social media rather than established state institutions.

One of the earliest controversies came during the joint sitting of Parliament on May 11, when Shah walked out while President Ramchandra Paudel was still delivering the government’s annual policies and programmes. The move was widely criticised by opposition parties and constitutional experts as a breach of parliamentary decorum and state protocol.

Another dispute followed the government’s decision to introduce a three percent tax on private education and healthcare services through the national budget. The proposal drew widespread public criticism, with opponents arguing that it would make essential services more expensive.

Amid growing pressure, the government withdrew the tax. However, the decision itself generated fresh criticism after Shah announced on Facebook that the “Education and Health Equity Tax” would be scrapped a day before the Cabinet formally approved the reversal, raising concerns that major executive decisions were being announced before completing official procedures.

Arjun Dhooj Aryal, an assistant professor at Tribhuvan University’s Central Department of Political Science, said governments must build consensus instead of relying on unilateral decisions.

“An executive should move forward by taking political parties, institutions and society into confidence,” Aryal said, arguing that governance through executive announcements and public messaging risks undermining institutional checks and balances.

The government’s handling of communal violence in Madhesh has emerged as another major subject of criticism.

The unrest began on July 26 in Dewanganj, Sunsari, after a dispute between two local communities escalated into violence. Police opened fire while trying to control the situation, killing Om Prakash Mehta. His death triggered protests that spread to several districts across Madhesh and Koshi provinces, disrupting normal life for nearly a week.

As tensions escalated, critics questioned the government’s response, saying senior leaders were slow to engage with the crisis. Neither Prime Minister Shah nor Home Minister Sudan Gurung visited the affected areas during the early days of the unrest.

Shah addressed the nation only on July 30, five days after the violence began. On the same day, Gurung travelled to Madhesh to begin talks with local leaders. By then, however, the unrest had spread to Golbazar in Siraha, where another person had died.

The week-long violence claimed four lives, including 15-year-old Ganesh Yadav of Aurahi Rural Municipality. Dozens of protesters and security personnel were injured, while public and private property was damaged in arson and vandalism. District administrations imposed curfews and prohibitory orders in several districts from Parsa to Dhanusha to contain the unrest.

In his address, Shah promised an impartial investigation into the deaths, pledged action against those responsible for inciting violence and appealed to the public not to spread communal hatred on social media. Peace talks led by the Home Ministry gradually helped restore normalcy.

Even so, the delayed response drew criticism from local residents, lawmakers and opposition leaders, who argued that quicker political intervention could have prevented further escalation.

The government’s handling of the crisis became a major political issue on July 30 when Rastriya Swatantra Party chair Rabi Lamichhane convened an all-party meeting at Singha Durbar to discuss the deteriorating security situation. Opposition leaders argued that such an initiative should have been led by the prime minister himself.

Before addressing the nation, Shah’s only public comments on the violence had come through Facebook, where he wrote that the government’s foremost duty was to ensure public security, punish those responsible and provide justice and compensation to victims.

Following the all-party meeting, opposition leaders accused the government of failing to provide timely leadership during one of the country’s most serious security crises in recent months.

Nepali Congress president Gagan Thapa questioned the prime minister’s absence during the early days of the unrest.

“Should a prime minister remain distant and act like an overlord during such a sensitive national crisis, when he should instead be leading the response?” Thapa told reporters after the meeting.

Aryal also argued that prompt political leadership could have reduced the scale of the violence.

“If the prime minister had intervened immediately with empathy and decisive leadership, the communal tension in Sunsari and neighbouring districts could have been contained much earlier,” he said.

Parliamentary absence and diplomatic controversy deepen scrutiny

Prime Minister Shah’s relationship with Parliament has become another major source of political contention, with opposition parties accusing him of repeatedly avoiding legislative scrutiny while choosing other platforms to defend key government decisions.

Since the new Parliament convened, opposition lawmakers have repeatedly demanded that the head of the government appear in the House of Representatives to answer questions on government policy, national security and executive actions. Instead, critics say, Prime Minister Shah has often delegated those responsibilities to ministers or responded through public speeches and social media.

The issue first came to the fore during deliberations on the government’s annual policies and programmes in May. The parliamentary agenda circulated before the sitting indicated that Shah would respond to lawmakers’ questions. However, the schedule was changed at the last minute, and Finance Minister Swarnim Wagle answered on behalf of the government.

The incident followed another controversy on May 11, when Shah walked out of the joint session of Parliament while President Ramchandra Paudel was still delivering the government’s policy address. His secretariat and Finance Minister Wagle later said the prime minister had left because of a sudden health problem, but opposition lawmakers remained unconvinced, particularly as Shah stayed away from key parliamentary proceedings during the budget session.

After weeks of absence following the presentation of the national budget on May 29, Shah unexpectedly appeared in the House of Representatives on May 31 to answer lawmakers’ questions.

Rather than easing tensions, the session triggered one of the government’s most significant diplomatic controversies.

While responding to questions on border management and Nepal’s territorial disputes with India, Shah told Parliament that he had learned after becoming prime minister that “not only has India encroached on Nepal’s land, but Nepal has also encroached on India’s land in multiple places.”

The remarks prompted immediate criticism from lawmakers across the political spectrum, who described the statement as unsubstantiated and potentially damaging to Nepal’s long-standing diplomatic position on border disputes.

Opposition parties demanded that the prime minister return to Parliament to clarify his remarks and apologise, arguing that such statements required clear evidence and careful diplomatic handling.

Instead of addressing the issue in the House, Shah responded weeks later at the inaugural convention of Rastriya Swatantra Party in Chitwan on June 21.

Speaking to party supporters, he defended his commitment to Nepal’s territorial claims and said there should be no doubt about his nationalism.

“When we raise border issues, the neighbouring country naturally shows interest,” Shah said. “We have evidence regarding Kalapani and Lipulekh. If we need to retrieve documents from the period of British rule, we will do so. We are not asking the British to mediate. We will resolve these matters directly with our neighbours.”

His remarks, however, did little to satisfy opposition lawmakers, who argued that explanations on matters of national importance should be delivered in Parliament rather than at a party gathering.

The issue resurfaced on July 30, when opposition parties again demanded the prime minister’s presence in the House, this time over the communal unrest in Sunsari and other districts of Madhesh.

Lawmakers from the Nepali Congress, CPN-UML, Nepali Communist Party, Rastriya Prajatantra Party and other parties protested in Parliament, accusing the government of failing to brief the legislature on one of the country’s most serious security crises in recent months.

NCP lawmaker Gopal Sharma said that as the sovereign representative body, Parliament had the right to receive a full account of the government’s handling of the violence.

“The Sunsari incident has shaken the entire country,” Sharma said in the House. “In such a sensitive situation, the prime minister should have come to Parliament to inform the sovereign House about the incident and the overall situation. But where is our prime minister?”

Opposition leaders argue that Shah’s repeated absence has weakened parliamentary accountability at a time when the government has been making far-reaching policy decisions.

Political analysts say the criticism is less about the number of appearances than about the message they send regarding the executive’s relationship with the legislature.

Under Nepal’s parliamentary system, they argue, the prime minister is expected to defend government policies, answer lawmakers’ questions and remain accountable to Parliament, particularly during national crises or controversies involving foreign policy.

Ordinances, appointments and allegations of executive overreach

Despite commanding the support of a coalition close to a two-thirds majority in Parliament, the Balendra Shah government has faced criticism for increasingly relying on ordinances and centralised decision-making instead of legislative processes.

The controversy began in April when the government abruptly prorogued a parliamentary session just a day after it had been summoned for April 30. Soon afterwards, the Cabinet recommended eight ordinances to President Ramchandra Paudel, four of which were promulgated.

The move prompted criticism from constitutional experts, who questioned why the government chose to bypass Parliament despite enjoying a comfortable majority.

Constitutional expert Bipin Adhikari said at the time that dissolving a session that had already been called solely to promulgate ordinances undermined parliamentary practice.

“If that was not the intention, the government should explain why it prorogued Parliament,” Adhikari told Kantipur. “A government with such a large majority should not avoid the legislature. It should be setting an example of parliamentary governance.”

The government’s use of the ordinances had immediate administrative consequences. On May 2, around 1,500 office bearers serving in public boards, state-owned enterprises and autonomous agencies were removed from their positions.

More than three months later, many of those vacancies remain unfilled, raising concerns over delays in decision-making and the functioning of several public institutions.

The appointments that have been made have also attracted criticism.

Although the government pledged to introduce a transparent, merit-based appointment system, opposition leaders and governance experts argue that several appointments have instead reflected political considerations.

One frequently cited example is the High Powered Committee for Integrated Development of the Bagmati Civilisation, where the government appointed Anand Singh Bhat as executive chairman despite another candidate topping the official merit list prepared by the selection committee.

Questions have also been raised over appointments to the Shahid Dashrath Chand University of Medical Sciences, the Security Printing Centre, the Guthi Sansthan, the Health Insurance Board, Nepal Scouts and the Tribhuvan University Service Commission.

Critics argue that some appointments favoured individuals with political links to the ruling Rastriya Swatantra Party, contradicting the administration’s promise to depoliticise public institutions.

Another recurring criticism concerns the growing influence of the prime minister’s secretariat.

Although the government won praise early in its tenure for reducing the number of ministries from 21 to 18, opponents say the savings were offset by allowing ministers to retain large personal secretariats staffed with political advisers.

The prime minister’s secretariat, in particular, has faced allegations of interfering in bureaucratic decisions, procurement processes and the work of independent institutions.

The most prominent example centres on the procurement of Nepal’s new electronic passports.

The Department of Passports awarded the contract to German firms Veridos and Mühlbauer on June 6, 2025. Members of the prime minister’s secretariat later questioned the procurement process, alleging financial irregularities and claiming the companies would be unable to deliver the passports on time.

On June 15, senior officials from the secretariat convened a meeting at the Prime Minister’s Office attended by representatives of the Department of Passports, the two German companies and senior officials of the Commission for the Investigation of Abuse of Authority (CIAA).

According to critics, the meeting placed pressure on the anti-graft body to investigate the procurement and initiate legal action against officials involved.

The CIAA arrested former department’s director general Tirtha Raj Aryal the same day and later filed corruption cases against 18 people, including civil servants and representatives of the German firms.

However, the government’s position came under renewed scrutiny on June 29 when the Special Court released Aryal and the other defendants on bail, citing insufficient grounds for continued detention.

Meanwhile, the German companies proceeded with the production and delivery of Nepal’s electronic passports, despite earlier claims that they would be unable to fulfil the contract.

Subsequent reports also alleged that the PMO had pressed the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the Department of Passports to cancel the procurement process.

The controversy intensified after Shah publicly defended the actions of his secretariat during the Rastriya Swatantra Party’s national convention in Chitwan on June 21.

Referring to the CIAA, he said that if necessary, authorities could question anti-corruption officials for “five hours” or even “five years”, adding that any such action would remain within the law.

The remarks prompted fresh criticism from opposition leaders and governance experts, who argued that independent constitutional bodies should be allowed to function without political pressure.

Demolitions, controversial appointments and a demoralised bureaucracy

Several of the Shah government’s domestic policies have also come under scrutiny, particularly its handling of informal settlements, the civil service and high-profile political appointments.

Less than a month after taking office, the government launched a drive to clear informal settlements along the Bagmati River and other waterways in the Kathmandu Valley, deploying bulldozers to demolish structures occupied by landless families.

The operation was criticised by rights groups and legal experts, who argued that the evictions were carried out without adequate rehabilitation plans or alternative housing for displaced residents. With the demolitions taking place at the start of the monsoon, hundreds of families were forced into temporary shelters, triggering protests that continued for months.

Writing in Kantipur on May 10, legal scholar Ritesh Panthi described the government’s approach as unconstitutional and inconsistent with the rights guaranteed to vulnerable communities.

The National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) also urged the government to halt forced evictions, protect the rights of displaced families and develop a comprehensive rehabilitation plan.

The controversy deepened after flooding inundated a temporary holding centre in Kirtipur on July 1. Gen Z activist Majid Ansari visited the site to assess conditions and distribute relief before being detained by police.

Human rights organisations and civil society groups condemned the incident after Ansari alleged he had been assaulted in custody. He was later admitted to Maharajgunj-based Teaching Hospital for treatment and released following intervention by the NHRC.

The case exposed divisions within the ruling coalition, with RSP lawmaker Sulabh Kharel publicly questioning the police response to the incident.

The government also faced criticism over a stricter enforcement of customs rules along the Nepal-India border.

Beginning in April, Armed Police Force personnel stationed at border crossings announced that goods worth more than Rs100 brought from India would be subject to customs duties and inspection.

The move angered residents of border districts, many of whom regularly cross into India for small household purchases. Business groups, including the Federation of Nepalese Chambers of Commerce and Industry, described the threshold as impractical and harmful to local economies.

Following protests from traders and local residents, enforcement of the measure was gradually relaxed in several border areas.

Questions have also persisted over the government’s decision to reappoint Home Minister Gurung.

Gurung resigned on April 22 after allegations relating to unexplained wealth and stock market transactions. The government subsequently formed an inquiry committee headed by former judge Achyut Prasad Bhandari.

On June 9, the Cabinet accepted the committee’s report, but did not make it public. Gurung was reappointed home minister on the same day, prompting opposition criticism over the government’s refusal to disclose the findings before restoring him to office.

Speaking in the National Assembly on June 15, Congress chief whip Padam Bahadur Pariyar questioned the decision, saying Parliament and the public had a right to know the contents of the investigation report before Gurung’s reinstatement.

The home minister’s return attracted further scrutiny after an NHRC panel investigating the Gen-Z protests of September 8 and 9 reportedly recommended action against him. NHRC Commissioner Lili Thapa later questioned whether investigations could remain impartial when an individual facing scrutiny headed the ministry responsible for law enforcement.

The government’s handling of another high-profile case also came under criticism after the Department of Money Laundering Investigation arrested former finance minister and CPN-UML Vice-Chair Bishnu Prasad Paudel on June 22.

Paudel spent 25 days in custody before the Special Court ordered his release on July 17, citing insufficient primary evidence to support the prosecution’s case.

Within the civil service, uncertainty over possible reforms has fuelled growing unease.

Reports that the government was considering mandatory retirement after 30 years of service or at the age of 55 prompted a wave of resignation requests from senior bureaucrats, although no such policy has been implemented.

The appointment of Govinda Bahadur Karki as chief secretary on July 8 also drew criticism after several more senior secretaries were overlooked. A day later, prime minister’s political adviser Asim Shah presided over the farewell ceremony for outgoing chief secretary Suman Raj Aryal, an unusual role for a political appointee that some former bureaucrats described as a breach of administrative convention.
